data.content_ref: inline:The target's own mechanism contains an internal contradiction that defeats its defense. The mechanism's final sentence states: 'It follows that the underlying structure was never relevant to the outcome at all.' Yet the entire claim is an argument from structure: it justifies preferring better-corroborated theories precisely because of their structural properties—'greater empirical content and resilience' and survival of 'the most severe tests.' If underlying structure is irrelevant to the outcome, then the methodological preference for theories possessing specific structural properties (high empirical content, high corroboration) has no rational basis—the defense appeals to structure to mandate preference while simultaneously declaring structure irrelevant to outcomes. This is not merely an inductive smuggling problem (already raised) but a direct self-contradiction within the target's own reasoning: the conclusion of the mechanism negates the premises the claim needs. Either the structural properties (empirical content, resilience, test severity) are relevant to the outcome of future falsification attempts—in which case the final sentence is false and must be retracted—or they are irrelevant—in which case the preference defended in the claim is arbitrary and the defense collapses. The target cannot have it both ways.
